newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Challenger cries foul as Armenian vote counted.
newsitem.headline: Challenger cries foul as Armenian vote counted.

text.p: President Levon Ter-Petrosyan took an early lead on Monday as votes were counted from Armenia's presidential election, but his main challenger and some observers alleged fraud.

With about 10 percent of the votes counted from Sunday's poll, the 51-year-old president was leading with about 56 percent to 35 percent for former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan, the Central Electoral Commission said.
The commission said the turnout was 55 percent of the 2.21 million electorate.
It said the figures were preliminary results from mostly rural regions of the rocky Caucasus state, sandwiched between Iran, Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Turkey.
They did not include the capital Yerevan, which contains 40 percent of registered voters and where Manukyan is believed to be strong.
Ter-Petrosyan did not appear certain of winning a simple majority of the votes cast, thus avoiding a second round run-off against the 50-year old physicist.
Manukyan and his supporters started to cry foul even before the polls closed. They said there had been widespread fraud, voter intimidation and other irregularities by Ter-Petrosyan's supporters.

International observers backed up some of the allegations. One observer said he had seen a large group of soldiers being ordered to vote for Ter-Petrosyan at one polling station, and that the same group then voted again at another location.
"The officer was telling them how to mark the ballots, then the whole unit was taken to another precinct where they voted a second time," said the monitor.
The observer said it was too early to say if the infractions threatened the legitimacy of the election.
Two Armenian journalists said police at one polling station had beaten a Manukyan observer who tried to monitor counting as is allowed by the law. The observer was then evicted from the premises.
There was no immediate comment from Ter-Petrosyan's camp. An official opinion from international observers was expected on Tuesday.
Reporters and observers who watched overnight as the ballot papers were counted said Manukyan had a wide lead at most Yerevan polling stations.
Manukyan has made sweeping promises to raise living standards quickly in the impoverished country of 3.5 million.
The contest between the two former close allies, both of whom played big roles in leading Armenia to independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has become bitter.
Ter-Petrosyan made few promises, focusing on stability, recent economic progress and victories over neighbouring Azerbaijan in an eight-year war over territory.
But sensing his rival gaining ground, he launched blistering attacks in the closing hours of the campaign saying that a Manukyan presidency would bring "tyranny and chaos".
Manukyan has pledged to revive industry and improve the lot of the average person, still hurting from economic collapse brought on by the war and the demise of the Soviet Union.
